clue.text: Rabbit — one name is 'bun'

blocks.note: first meaning: in games slang a rabbit is a hopeless player, a duffer who muffs every chance
second meaning: a soft round bread roll that also goes by the name bun

explanation.surface: Someone introducing a pet rabbit whose name is Bun.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'bun' look like a bunny's pet name, but it is the bakery word; 'rabbit' is the sporting insult for a poor player.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are recorded: a clumsy duffer at games, and a small soft bread cake akin to a bun.

clue.text: Free article from the B.B.C.

indicators.note: taking something from a word means removing it, so the article is subtracted

blocks.note: the indefinite article
Auntie, or Auntie Beeb, is the British Broadcasting Corporation's affectionate nickname

explanation.surface: A free piece published by the BBC's website or magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free article' reads as a giveaway item; in fact 'Free' is the definition and 'article from' tells you to remove A from the BBC's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: To free something tied up is to loosen its knots, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Bird grazing?

blocks.note: surface reading: a bird pecking at food on the ground
setter's reading: grazing is eating the food a meadow offers, read as two words, meadow and food

explanation.walkthrough: Split the name into FIELD and FARE: fare is food, so grazing is literally field fare.
explanation.definitionFit: The fieldfare is a large thrush that winters in Britain, feeding in open fields.

clue.text: Count more dead

blocks.note: first meaning: to total things up, as a verb
second meaning: comparative of numb, having less feeling, as fingers go dead in the cold

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as numb-er, the comparative adjective, rather than the noun; the pronunciation changes too.
explanation.definitionFit: To number items is to count them, and a hand gone more dead with cold is numb-er.

clue.text: Macaroni and ginger-beer imbibed by bird

blocks.note: pop is a fizzy soft drink
a drink imbibed by someone ends up in them
a jay is a bird of the crow family

explanation.surface: A bird sipping ginger beer alongside a plate of pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imbibed by' supplies IN literally: the drink is in the bird. A macaroni was an 18th-century English dandy, not the pasta.
explanation.definitionFit: A popinjay is a vain, showy fop, which is exactly what the eighteenth-century macaroni was.

clue.text: Party that, in power, tend to be undisciplined

indicators.note: unruly letters will not keep their order, so the preceding words must be rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: A political party which, once in government, tends to lose discipline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks like a political noun, but it is a verb: to celebrate wildly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to go out and celebrate riotously, which is what partying hard is.

clue.text: Henry participates in rustic game

indicators.note: one who takes part in something is inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
a country labourer

explanation.surface: A man called Henry joining in a country pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' looks like a pastime, but it means hunted birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Pheasants are shot for sport and eaten, the classic example of game birds.

clue.text: Verse included in Christmas story

indicators.note: something included is placed within the following word

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for verse
Noel is another word for Christmas

explanation.surface: A Christmas tale with a poem embedded in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A novel is a book-length piece of prose fiction, a long story.

clue.text: Bill, a print worker some go along with

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
comp is printers' slang for a compositor, who sets type
as in 'have you any?'

explanation.surface: A bill and a printer that some people go along with.
explanation.walkthrough: A compositor, or comp, was the tradesman who set metal type by hand for printing.
explanation.definitionFit: To accompany someone is to travel with them, a direct synonym of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Let marines loose to reduce resistance. . .

indicators.note: let loose, the letters run free and fall into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: An order to unleash the marines and break down enemy opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resistance' suggests armed opposition, but it is the drag of air or water.
explanation.definitionFit: Streamlining shapes a body smoothly so that air or water drag on it falls.

clue.text: . . . instead of failing

blocks.note: first meaning: the Latin preposition meaning in place of
second meaning: a moral weakness or fault

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on from 9 across, so it reads as streamlining instead of failing; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Vice is used formally to mean in place of, and as a noun means a moral fault or weakness.

clue.text: Man, a doctor, is abroad, providing capital support

indicators.note: abroad tells you to translate the word into a foreign language, here French

blocks.note: he is the male pronoun
taken as written
standard abbreviation
est is French for is

explanation.surface: A doctor working overseas who props up the national capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' means head, not a city or money.
explanation.definitionFit: A headrest is a cushion or bracket that supports the head, which is capital in its original Latin sense.

clue.text: August, when melons are fully developed

indicators.note: something developed has changed its form, so the letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: the fodder

explanation.surface: August is the month when melons ripen fully.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital A makes 'August' look like the month; it is the adjective meaning dignified.
explanation.definitionFit: August as an adjective means grand and dignified, close to grave and stately in tone.

clue.text: British water less weighty than Continental

indicators.note: less means minus, so the following piece is taken away

blocks.note: a ton is a large weight
Lake Balaton in Hungary, the largest lake in central Europe, a Continental water

explanation.surface: A comparison of British and European water by weight.
explanation.walkthrough: The Continental lake loses the weight: Balaton less TON. Bala Lake (Llyn Tegid) is the largest natural lake in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Bala is a lake in north Wales, so it is a body of water in Britain.

clue.text: 13 turned flower to stone

indicators.note: turned round, the referenced answer is read from back to front

blocks.note: the answer to 13 across
the aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: Something that turned a flower into stone.
explanation.walkthrough: Turn the Welsh lake from 13 across round to get ALAB, then add the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabaster is a soft, white, translucent mineral carved for ornaments, a kind of stone.

clue.text: Both hot and cold wash eliciting a show of appreciation

blocks.note: H and C, the labels on hot and cold taps
as waves lap or wash against a shore

explanation.surface: A hot-and-cold wash so good it earns a round of applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both' signals that AND itself is kept between the two tap letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Clapping the hands together is the usual gesture of applause, a way to show approval.

clue.text: Angry about ford, perhaps

blocks.note: cross means annoyed
as in a quarrel over money

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed about Ford, the car maker or the president.
explanation.walkthrough: The lower-case 'ford' suggests a name; it is a shallow place to wade across a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A ford is one example of a place where you pass from one side of a river to the other.

clue.text: Kind of bowl made of metal, cast

blocks.note: gold is a precious metal
to cast a line is to angle

explanation.surface: A bowl made of cast metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' looks like metal-founding, which pairs with 'metal'; it is the angler's cast.
explanation.definitionFit: A goldfish bowl is the round glass tank for pet fish, so the answer names that kind of bowl.

clue.text: Be far too embarrassed, being not fully dressed

indicators.note: someone embarrassed is flustered and disordered, so the letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone mortified at being caught half-dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Going without shoes or socks leaves your outfit incomplete, a playful sense of underdressed.

clue.text: Stone carried by persons unknown

blocks.note: a load carried by a horse is on it
Y and X, the algebraist's unknowns, standing for two unnamed people

explanation.surface: A gemstone smuggled away by unidentified people.
explanation.walkthrough: Mathematical unknowns are a standard source of X, Y and Z.
explanation.definitionFit: Onyx is a banded variety of chalcedony used for cameos, a semi-precious stone.

clue.text: Ruffled horse carries rider at the start

indicators.note: a horse carrying something has it on board, so one piece sits within another
only the opening letter of the named word is wanted

blocks.note: a filly is a young female horse
first letter of rider

explanation.surface: A flustered horse with a jockey up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruffled' suggests an upset horse; it means trimmed with ruffles.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruffle is a gathered strip of fabric, so ruffled clothing is decorated with frills.

clue.text: Everyone joins in poor song

indicators.note: to join in is to enter something, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: everyone means all
of low quality

explanation.surface: Everybody singing along with a dreadful song.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballad is a narrative song or a slow sentimental popular one.

clue.text: I have to catch the others, left at the start and the end

indicators.note: this places the following piece in front of everything else

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left

blocks.clueFragment: I have to catch the others
blocks.note: in the game of tag, the one who must catch everyone else says I'm it

explanation.surface: A player in a chasing game explaining the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase about catching is a cryptic paraphrase of the playground cry, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: The limit is the furthest point that can be reached, as in being the end of what is bearable.

clue.text: Meeting to discuss the office dance

blocks.note: works is a place of work, as in gasworks
a hop is an informal dance

explanation.surface: A meeting called to talk about the office party.
explanation.definitionFit: A workshop is a session where a group gathers to discuss and practise a topic together.

clue.text: A very small quantity found in a cat

blocks.note: first meaning: a tiny amount
second meaning: another name for the snow leopard

explanation.surface: A tiny amount of something discovered inside a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter uses the same clue twice: here it is two meanings joined by 'found in'; at 25 across it is a definition plus wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An ounce is a small unit of weight, hence a scrap, and also the snow leopard of Central Asia.

clue.text: A very small quantity found in a cat

blocks.note: taken as written
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A tiny amount of something discovered inside a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: The same wording also clues 24 down; there both halves are meanings, here 'a cat' builds the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An atom is figuratively the tiniest scrap of anything, as in not an atom of truth.

clue.text: Diverted train with lever beside the point

indicators.note: a diverted train is sent off its usual route, so the letters go another way

blocks.note: part of the fodder
part of the fodder

explanation.surface: A train switched onto another line by a signal lever beside the points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the point' suggests railway points, which a lever switches; it is the point of an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Something beside the point has no bearing on the matter in hand, an idiom for unconnected.

clue.text: Woman thrown up and down

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for woman
retched means heaved or vomited

explanation.surface: A woman tossed into the air and dropped again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up and down' reads as a single phrase of movement, but 'down' alone is the definition, meaning miserable.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling down is feeling low and unhappy, and a wretched person is in deep misery.

clue.text: Ball held by Miss Piggy — or Kermit

indicators.note: the letters are clasped within the words that follow, straddling them

blocks.note: the end of Piggy, then or, then the start of Kermit

explanation.surface: Miss Piggy or Kermit the Frog holding a ball, Muppet-style.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a yorker is a delivery pitched right at the batsman's feet, hard to hit.
explanation.definitionFit: A yorker is a type of delivery bowled in cricket, so it is one kind of ball.
